content:
<Rep. Maxine Waters, Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez, Rep. Bill Foster, Rep. Al Green, Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, Rep. Joyce Beatty, Rep. Ayanna Pressley, Rep. Rashida Tlaib>: At a time of unprecedented AI risk, H.R. 4801 would give companies free rein to experiment on consumers and investors on their own terms. This legislation directs the Fed, FDIC, OCC, SEC, CFPB, NCUA, and FHFA to each establish an AI Innovation Lab that would allow companies to experiment with AI projects without complying with certain regulations or being subject to enforcement actions. The bill allows entities to propose their own alternative method to comply with regulations that they want waived or modified. All the company must do is ``explain'' how their AI project would meet certain characteristics. However, there is no way for the regulators to look under the hood and make sure these statements are accurate. Instead, there is presumed approval by the regulators with no opportunity for public comment.
Furthermore, this bill would also authorize the private sector entity, and not the regulator, to set the timeline, size, scope, and growth of the project. The definition of the project is broad, allowing these entities to waive or modify regulations on a wide range of activities, as long as the project ``makes substantial use of AI.'' Under this bill for example, companies could waive anti-discrimination laws and regulations, including the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act, the Fair Housing Act, and the Community Reinvestment Act. There also is no restriction on companies waiving key investor protections, like the fiduciary duty requirement of the Investment Adviser Act of 1940, which guards against mismanagement by financial advisors, or market manipulation laws and regulations. Additionally, there are no limitations or safeguards in H.R. 4801 that protect consumers, small businesses, or financial markets from harm.
To make matters worse, this legislation fundamentally ignores the fears and concerns the American public has in light of the latest AI developments. In recent years, companies have integrated Generative AI (Gen AI) and agentic AI (AAI or AI agents) into various facets of American's lives.\1\ While AI technology may have some benefits, the American public is concerned about the scale of its risks. In fact, voters overwhelmingly support the regulation of AI. Polling shows that 97% of Americans think that, ``AI safety and security should be subject to rules and regulations.''\2\ Increasing regulation of AI has bipartisan support--77% of voters, including 75% of Republicans, say ``government should do more to regulate AI.''\3\ This bill does the exact opposite. Furthermore, this legislation does not grapple with AI's current impact on the workforce and its potential for large-scale disruption. As companies apply for the regulatory waivers available pursuant to H.R. 4801 and widely launch their AI projects, these companies have no requirement test the impact of the project on the affected workers or on the broader labor market. Additionally, this bill is silent on the environmental consequences and harmful health implications that AI data centers are having on local communities.
\1\Gen AI goes beyond analyzing data, and when prompted can create original content such as text, images, videos, music, and more. See What is generative AI?, IBM (Apr. 20, 2023). Although Gen AI and AAI both rely on LLMs as a foundation, Gen AI technology focuses on creating new content based on learned patterns, while AAI or AI agents go further by autonomously and proactively executing complex tasks. See, FinRegLab, The Next Wave Arrives: Agentic AI in Financial Services (Sept. 2025); and IBM, What is agentic AI? (accessed Sept. 14, 2025).
\2\Years of Polling Show Overwhelming Voter Support for a Crackdown on AI, Public Citizen (Nov. 21, 2025).
\3\Id.
The challenges from Gen AI and AAI are further exacerbated as AI model capabilities grow exponentially. On April 7, Anthropic announced information on its Claude Mythos Preview, a new general purpose language model, which the company describes as ``extremely autonomous'' and extraordinarily capable at computer security tasks, software coding, and complex reasoning objectives.\4\ According to Anthropic, Claude Mythos Preview ``has already found thousands of high-severity vulnerabilities, including some in every major operating system and web browser. . . . The fallout-for economies, public safety, and national security--could be severe.''\5\ These warnings were followed by urgent and unprecedented meetings between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Fed Chair Jerome Powell and the CEOs of nation's largest banks\6\ and meetings between Anthropic and the White House to discuss AI safety and risks.\7\ World leaders and regulators continue to express concerns regarding the scale and speed of Mythos' and other AI models' capabilities.\8\ Yet surprisingly, this bill contains no reference to these developments and instead could threaten our financial system's safety and soundness at a time when Congress' focus should be on security.
\4\Anthropic holds Mythos model due to hacking AXIOS (Apr. 7, 2026); Anthropic, Project Glasswing (accessed Apr. 24, 2026).
\5\Anthropic, Project Glasswing (accessed Apr. 24, 2026).
\6\Bessent, Powell warned bank CEOs about Anthropic model risks, sources say, Reuters (Apr. 9, 2026); Bessent and Powell's A.I. Anxiety, New York Times (Apr. 10, 2026).
\7\Anthropic's New A.I. Model Sets Off Global Alarms, New York Times (Apr. 22, 2026).
\8\Global regulators trail banks in AI as Mythos raises oversight concerns, report finds, Reuters (Apr. 28, 2026).
During the markup, Democrats offered four amendments aimed at alleviating the deficiencies within the legislation, all of which were rejected by Republicans:\9\
\9\House Committee on Financial Services, Committee Markup, 19th Cong. (May 13, 2026).
• Ranking Member Waters' amendment would
prevent the bill from taking effect until there is a
study by Treasury, in consultation with the other
regulators in the bill, that confirms that the bill
would not increase risks to consumers from models like
Mythos;
• Rep. Lynch's first amendment adds two new
criteria that an A.I. system must meet to qualify for a
test project: (1) it must be explainable to users and
consumers; and (2) must not have unreliable or unfair
outputs;
• Rep. Lynch's second amendment requires
applicants to explain how their A.I. test project will
reduce consumer costs as a condition of approval, and
report this information to the appropriate agency; and,
• Rep. Lynch's third amendment clarifies that
financial regulatory agencies retain full enforcement
and penalty authority, if a person is harmed as a
result of an AI test project.
H.R. 4801 is opposed by 90 civil rights, consumer, labor, technology, and other advocacy groups.\10\
\10\Americans for Financial Reform, Letters to Congress: AFR Joined by 89 Groups to Oppose Financial AI Sandbox Giveaway (May 12, 2026).
For all of these reasons, we oppose H.R. 4801.
Maxine Waters,
Ranking Member.
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Bill Foster,
Al Green,
Emanuel Cleaver, II,
Joyce Beatty,
